title.en: The Night on Huanacauri: Youths Ask Leave to Become Knights
title.zh: 瓦納考里之夜:少年求賜騎士之名

region.en: Huanacauri hill, south of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科以南瓦納考里山(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the month of Ccapac Raymi the youths about to receive their arms went to the huaca called Huanacauri, their principal huaca - the brother, as was said, of Manco Ccapac, whence they descend - to offer sacrifice and ask permission to receive knighthood. They passed the night on the hill where the huaca was kept, in memory of the journey which their ancestors commenced from that spot, and returned next day bearing loads of straw for their parents to sit on, having fasted on the road.
summary.zh: 卡帕克雷米月,受武之少年往瓦納考里瓦卡——此為其至聖瓦卡,乃曼科·卡帕克之「兄弟」,族人皆出其後——獻祭並求賜騎士之名。他們夜宿藏神像之山,以紀念祖先自該地啟程的旅程;次日攜草束而歸,供父母坐臥,一路齋戒。

sensitivity.note: Initiation vigil at the ancestral huaca-stone; Molina defers the stone-brother tradition to his history of the Incas (cut separately).

passages.text: The youths who were about to receive their arms went to the huaca called Huanacauri, to offer sacrifice, and to ask permission to receive knighthood. For this was their principal huaca, the brother, as was said, of Manco Ccapac, whence they descend.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of October (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The youths who were to be armed as knights passed that night on the hill of Huanacauri, where the huaca was kept, in memory of the journey which their ancestors commenced from that spot. On the next day they returned in the afternoon, bringing with them loads of straw, on which their parents and relations might sit. On this day the youths fasted; and the month was passed in preparing many kinds of chicha for the festival.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of October (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this time, and indeed throughout the year, the priests of the Creator, of the Sun, and of Thunder, and those who had charge of the huaca of Huanacauri, made three daily sacrifices; offering up three sheep, one in the morning, one at noon, and a third at night. The persons also who had charge of the embalmed bodies never came forth to offer up the food and pour out the chicha dedicated to them, such as they used when they were alive; these they consumed, because they held for very truth the doctrine of the immortality of the soul, and said that wherever the soul might be, it would receive the food and eat as when alive.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of October (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Huarachicu: Manco Capac's Sons Armed as Knights
title.zh: 瓦拉奇庫:曼科·卡帕克子孫受武為騎士

region.en: Huanacauri hill and Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦納考里山與庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the feast of the Lord Inca the youths of pure Inca descent received the huaracas, bags and breeches: the huaracas of aloe fibre and sheep's sinew, it was said, were worn by their ancestors when they came forth from Paccari-tampu. Sacrificing five lambs on Huanacauri, the Tarpuntays blew wool into the air praying 'O Huanacauri! our father, may the Creator, the Sun, and the Thunder ever remain young'; uncles and parents whipped the youths' arms and legs, saying 'Be brave as I have been'; the knights raced to Anahuarqui, whose huaca ran like a lion in the tradition handed down from the time of the deluge; at Raurana, whose huaca of two stone falcons was instituted by Pachacutec Yupanqui and beautified by Huascar with falcons brought from the idol of the Indians of Maras, the breeches and golden ear-pieces were given. Manco Ccapac instituted the feast for his son Sinchi Rocca, and the taqui huari, sung only at this festival, was given to Manco Ccapac by the Creator when he came forth from the Cave of Tampu.
summary.zh: 在「印加之宴」,純印加血統的少年接受瓦拉卡(吊索)、楚斯帕(小袋)與瓦拉(褲)。據說瓦拉卡以龍舌蘭纖維與羊筋製成,先祖自帕卡里坦波走出時便佩戴此物。在瓦納考里獻五羔祭後,祭司向空中吹羊毛,禱曰:「瓦納考里,我們的父親,願造物主、太陽與雷永葆青春!」叔伯父母鞭打少年手足,曰:「像我當年那樣勇敢!」騎士們在阿納瓦爾基賽跑——相傳自洪水時代起,此瓦卡如獅般奔跑;在勞拉納山,神廟供兩隻石隼,係帕查庫特克·尤潘琪所立,瓦伊納·卡帕克又自馬拉斯人偶像處取隼飾之。受武者於此得褲、金耳飾與羽冠。此節由曼科·卡帕克為其子辛奇·羅卡而設;「瓦里」之歌乃造物主在曼科走出坦波洞穴時所授,唯此節可唱。

sensitivity.note: Full initiation sequence from Molina's compilation; the lineage rules exclude non-Inca youths, recorded as given.

passages.text: Each of the youths who were about to be armed had a sheep prepared for sacrifice. They all went, with their relations, to the hill called Huanacauri. That night they slept at the foot of the hill, at a place called Matahua, and at sunrise, all fasting, they ascended the hill until they came to the huaca Huanacauri. When they reached the top of the hill, the Tarpuntays took five lambs and sacrificed them before the huaca, then divided the wool among the youths who were about to be made knights. The youths and chiefs then blew the wool into the air while the sacrifices were being consumed, with these words: 'O Huanacauri! our father, may the Creator, the Sun, and the Thunder ever remain young, and never become old. May thy son the Ynca always retain his youth, and grant that he may prosper in all he undertakes. And to us, thy sons and descendants who now celebrate this festival, grant that we may ever be in the hands of the Creator, of the Sun, of the Thunder, and in thy hands.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac Raymi (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the ninth hour of the day they put huaracas and bags called chuspas into the hands of the youths, and on presenting them with the huaracas they said: 'Now that our father Huanacauri has given the huaracas as a sign of valour, live henceforth as brave men.' They were made of aloe fibre and the sinews of sheep, and it was said that their ancestors, when they came forth from Paccari-tampu, wore them. Then they walked on until they came to a ravine called Quiras-manta, where they were met by the uncles and parents and chiefs, who whipped them on the arms and legs, saying, 'Be brave as I have been, and receive these gifts that you may imitate me.' Then they chaunted a song called Huari.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac Raymi (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The reason why they went to the huaca of Anahuarqui to perform a sacrifice was that, on this day, they had to run a race, to try which was the best runner. The tradition had been handed down from the time of the deluge that this huaca ran like a lion. The youthful knights stood in a row before the huaca of Anahuarqui, behind them a second row of arm bearers, and in their rear a third row whose duty it was to aid those who fell; in front of all was an Indian very gaily dressed who gave the word. They all began to run at full speed and with all their force; those who fell or fainted were assisted by the men in the rear, but some died of the falls. Those who reached the goal received drink from the maidens, and drank as they ran.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac Raymi (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The huaca of Raurana consisted of two falcons in stone, placed upon an altar on the summit of the hill. It was instituted by Pachacutec Ynca Yupanqui as the place where they should receive the breeches which they call huara. This huaca was at first the idol of the Indians of Maras, and Huascar Ynca caused the falcons to be brought here to beautify it. Manco Ccapac instituted this feast, and caused these ceremonies to be observed in the case of his son Sinchi Rocca. With reference to the taqui so often repeated in the ceremony, they say that, in the time of Manco Ccapac, when he came forth from the Cave of Tampu, it was given to him by the Creator with a command that it should be sung at this festival, and at no other.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac Raymi (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Chocanaco: Hanan against Hurin in the Thistle-Seed Battle
title.zh: 喬卡納科:哈南對烏林的薊籽之戰

region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: On the first day of Camay-quilla the newly armed knights of the lineages of Hanan Cuzco and Hurin Cuzco came into the great square with slings and hurled coco - the missiles found on certain thistles - against one another, at times coming to close quarters to prove the muscles of their arms, until the Inca, who was present, rose up and restored order. It was called chocanaco, a trial of strength to see who were the strongest and bravest.
summary.zh: 卡馬伊基利亞月初一,新受武的哈南庫斯科與烏林庫斯科兩世系騎士各執吊索入大廣場,互擲「科科」(一種薊上的籽實),時或近身角力以較臂力,直至在場的印加王起身喝止。此謂「喬卡納科」,較力之戲,以試誰最強最勇。

sensitivity.note: Martial game opening the December rites; the Hanan/Hurin duality is central to Cuzco social myth.

passages.text: On the first day of the month, those who had been armed as knights, as well those of the lineage of Hanan Cuzco as of Hurin Cuzco, came out into the square, with slings in their hands called huaraca, and the youths of Hanan Cuzco hurled against those of Hurin Cuzco; their missiles were called coco, which are found on certain thistles. At times they came to close quarters, to prove the muscles of their arms; until the Ynca, who was present, rose up and restored order. They called this chocanaco, and it was a trial of strength, to see who were the strongest and bravest.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Charcoal and Toads: Souls with the Creator or with Supay
title.zh: 炭與蟾蜍:歸造物主之魂與墮蘇帕伊之魂

region.en: Heaven above and the place of punishment below (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 上天與受罰之所(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Food and drink were offered to the embalmed dead as if they were alive, saying: 'When you were alive you used to eat and drink of this; may your soul now receive it and feed on it, wheresoever you may be.' For they believed and held it for certain that souls did not die, but that those of good men went to rest with the Creator, who would see them from heaven; they charged their families to perform all they had left them to do. But there was a place of punishment for bad men, where they were tormented by demons called Supay: there they suffered much hunger and thirst, and their food was charcoal, snakes, toads, and other things of that kind; while those who went to heaven ate and drank the best that the Creator had, and also received the food and liquor their relations offered up.
summary.zh: 人們向死者木乃伊供上食物與酒,如同其生前:說「你生前曾如此飲食,願你的靈魂今在何處都能領受而食之」。因他們確信靈魂不死,善人之魂歸造物主安息,自天上眷顧子孫,臨終時囑咐家人完成遺命。惡人之魂則墮入受罰之所,為名喚「蘇帕伊」的惡魔所折磨:飢渴交迫,所食者為炭、蛇、蟾蜍之類;而升天者得享造物主所有之至美飲食,亦能領受親人所供之食。

sensitivity.note: Andean eschatology as recorded by a missionary observer; 'Supay' later became the name for the Christian devil - here it is the native term for punishing demons.

passages.text: For this feast they brought all the huacas into the square, as well as the bodies of the dead Yncas, to drink with them; placing those who had belonged to the Hanan Cuzco on the side where that lineage was stationed, and the same with those of Hurin Cuzco. Then they brought food and drink to the dead bodies, as if they were alive, saying: 'When you were alive you used to eat and drink of this; may your soul now receive it and feed on it, wheresoever you may be.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: For they believed and held it for certain that souls did not die, but that those of good men went to rest with the Creator. When they died they declared this belief, and charged their families and relations to perform all that they had left them to do, and that they would see them from heaven. They also believed that there was a place of punishment for bad men, where they were tormented by demons called Supay. They said that those who went there suffered much hunger and thirst, and that their food was charcoal, snakes, toads, and other things of that kind. Those who went to heaven, on the other hand, ate and drank the best that the Creator had, and they also received the food and liquor which their relations offered up.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Moro-urco: The Four-Coloured Cable Wound Like a Serpent
title.zh: 莫羅-烏爾科:四色繩索如蛇盤繞

region.en: Moro-urco house near the temple of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽神廟旁莫羅-烏爾科之屋(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At the full moon of December the people went to the house called Moro-urco near the houses of the Sun, to take out a very long cable woven in four colours, black, white, red and yellow, with a stout ball of red wool at the end. Every one took hold of it, men on one side and women on the other, performing the taqui called yaqauyra; coming to the square they made their reverences to the huacas and the Inca, and kept going round and round until they were the shape of a spiral shell. Then they dropped the cable on the ground and left it coiled up like a snake. A lamb was sacrificed for the cable and for rain and the winter time, saying to the winter: 'Why hast thou rained?'
summary.zh: 十二月望月之夜,人民齊往太陽神廟旁的「莫羅-烏爾科」之屋,取出一條極長的繩索——以黑、白、紅、黃四色織成,末端繫一紅色羊毛大球。男女分列兩側,共執此繩,且行且歌。入廣場拜過瓦卡與印加王後,眾人繞行不止,直至隊形成螺旋貝狀,然後將繩索擲於地上,任其盤繞如蛇。為繩索與雨水獻祭一羔,並向冬天發問:「你為何降雨?」

sensitivity.note: The coiled four-coloured cable (huascar) is tagged to the world-serpent cluster for its serpent-coil imagery; the tag is interpretive.

passages.text: The rest of the people had gone to a house called Moro-urco, near the houses of the Sun, to take out a very long cable which was kept there, woven in four colours, black, white, red, and yellow, at the end of which there was a stout ball of red wool. Every one took hold of it, the men on one side, and the women on the other, performing the taqui called yaqauyra. When they came to the square, after making reverences to the huacas and the Ynca, they kept going round and round until they were the shape of a spiral shell. Then they dropped the huascar on the ground, and left it coiled up like a snake. They called this cable Moro-urco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Presently, they brought a lamb to be sacrificed for the cable, and for rain, and the winter time, saying to the winter: 'Why hast thou rained?' From noon to sunset was passed in rejoicings, and in drinking with the huacas and dead bodies.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Mojocati: The Year's Sacrifices Sent Down the River to Ollantay-tampu
title.zh: 莫霍卡蒂:歲祭順流送至歐雁台

region.en: Capi-mayu river, Cuzco to Ollantay-tampu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科卡皮河至歐雁台(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In December they collected all kinds of food, ajis, coca, cloths, shoes, llautus, plumes, sheep, flowers, gold and silver, and all the ashes of the year's sacrifices, and threw them into the dammed-up river Capi-mayu; the first dam was thrown down and the water rushed out with such fury that it carried the other dams away with it and all the sacrifices. Indians stationed with torches along the ten-league route by night accompanied the offerings to the bridge of Ollantay-tampu over the great river flowing to the North Sea, where two bags of coca were thrown from the bridge as the sacrifices flowed past. The reason given was that, as the Creator had granted them a good year, they should offer these things that they might not appear ungrateful. Those who had gone furthest carried salt lances and falcons; the laggards carried salt toads, and the people laughed at them.
summary.zh: 十二月,人們收齊各色食物、辣椒、古柯袋、衣裳、鞋履、勞圖頭帶、羽冠、羊、花、金銀,以及全年祭祀積存的灰燼,投入築壩蓄水的卡皮河。推倒第一道壩,洪水洶湧而出,連同諸壩與祭品一併沖走。沿途村落居民持火把排列於十萊格的夜路上,護送祭品直至歐雁台大橋——橋下大河奔向北海。祭物流過時,自橋上投入兩袋古柯。其理由是:造物主既賜他們豐年,便當以所得之物還祭,以免顯得不感恩。行得最遠者手持鹽製長矛與隼,落後者捧鹽製蟾蜍,惹得眾人哄笑。

sensitivity.note: The December river-sending rite; tagged with world-renewal as the year's accumulated sacra are washed to the sea.

passages.text: A small river flows through the centre of Cuzco called Capi-mayu and Huaca-puncu-mayu. In the ravines above the town they constructed dams to confine the water, although it was winter, in order that it might bear away the sacrifices with greater force. On this day they collected all kinds and sorts of food, all the different sorts of ajis, great quantities of bags of coca, all kinds of cloths of different colours and shoes, llautus and plumes, sheep, flowers, gold and silver, and every other sort of thing that they used, as well as all the ashes and cinders of all the sacrifices that had been preserved throughout the year.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: All these things were thrown into the river, the first dam was thrown down, and the water rushed out with such fury that it carried the other dams away with it, and all the sacrifices. Many people were assembled on both sides of the river, outside the city of Cuzco, at a place called Pumap-chupa. The Indians on both sides of the river were commanded by the Lord Ynca, who was present, to go with the sacrifices to Ollantay-tampu, ten leagues from Cuzco by the round. Indians of the villages by which they had to pass were stationed at intervals with torches, in order to give light during the night, and no part of the sacrifices was allowed to remain in the river. When they reached the bridge of Ollantay-tampu, over a great river flowing to the North Sea, they threw two bags of coca, called pilculuncu paucar uncu, from the bridge as the sacrifices flowed past.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The reason for throwing these sacrifices into the river was that, as the Creator of all things had granted them a good year, it seemed well that, out of the things that he had given them, they should offer these sacrifices, that they might not appear ungrateful, beseeching him to receive them, wheresoever he might please to be. Those who had gone furthest carried in their hands lances and falcons made of salt; while those who lagged behind had toads made of salt, as a sign that they had gone slowly, which made the people laugh at them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of December (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Mama Huaco's First Maize: The Farm of Sausiru
title.zh: 瑪瑪·瓦科的初植玉米:薩烏西魯田

region.en: Farm of Sausiru beneath the fortress of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科要塞下薩烏西魯田(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the harvest month of Ayrihuay the newly armed knights went to the farm of Sausiru, beneath the citadel, to fetch the reaped maize; there, they say, Mama-huaco, the sister of Manco Ccapac, sowed the first maize. The farm was cultivated every year for the body of this Mama-huaco, making from the crop the chicha necessary for the service of the embalmed body, which was delivered to those who had charge of it. The maize of the harvests of the Creator, the Sun, the Moon, the Thunder, the Ynca, Huanacauri and all the dead lords was brought in small baskets, singing a chaunt called yaravi and dressed in gay clothes.
summary.zh: 收穫月艾里瓦伊,新受武的騎士前往要塞下的薩烏西魯田運取已收之玉米。相傳瑪瑪·瓦科——曼科·卡帕克之姊妹——在此播下第一粒玉米。此田歲歲耕種,專為瑪瑪·瓦科之遺體:以其收成釀奇恰酒,交由管理木乃伊之人以供祭祀。造物主、太陽、月亮、雷神、印加王、瓦納考里及歷代先王的收穫玉米,皆由人們盛於小籃,身著華服,唱著名為「雅拉維」的哀歌,一一運回。

sensitivity.note: Etiological farm of the first maize, tied to the ancestral mother-warrior Mama Huaco; gendered founder narrative preserved from a male-priest compilation.

passages.text: The month of April was called Ayrihuay. In it they reaped the crops and got in the harvests. Those who had received arms as knights went to the farm of Sausiru, to fetch the maize that had been reaped there, which is beneath the citadel. It is here they say that Mama-huaco, the sister of Manco Ccapac, sowed the first maize.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of April (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They cultivated this farm every year for the body of this Mama-huaco, making from the crop the chicha that was necessary for the service of the body, and delivering this chicha to those who had charge of the body, which was embalmed. Then, in their order, they brought the maize of the harvests of the Creator, the Sun, the Moon, the Thunder, the Ynca, and Huanacauri, and of all the dead lords. They brought it in small baskets, singing a chaunt called yaravi, and dressed in gay clothes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of April (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the rest of the people of Cuzco went to bring in this maize, except on the first day, when it was brought by the youths who had received knighthood. The priests, called Tarpuntays, offered up a lamb in sacrifice, beseeching the Creator ever to grant them good harvests. This lasted for four days, after which they went back to their farms; and so the year ended.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of April (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)
